ops.text: Three moving parts, all started by one SIGTERM, the only signal Kubernetes sends before SIGKILL. First, the handler flips a readiness flag so /readyz returns 503 at once; this is the 'stop new traffic' step, and the process keeps serving while the load balancer stops routing to it. Second, after DRAIN_DELAY_SECONDS (5 s in Example 21; it plays the part of a preStop sleep) the handler chains to uvicorn's own: uvicorn installs its signal handlers before it imports the app and runs the lifespan, so a handler that replaces them without chaining means uvicorn never starts its drain and the process waits for SIGKILL. uvicorn then stops accepting and finishes in-flight HTTP; --timeout-graceful-shutdown 20 bounds that wait, so delay plus drain stays inside the 30-second grace period. Third, FastAPI's lifespan shutdown block (after the yield) runs once HTTP has drained: that is where you stop consumers (an aiokafka consumer commits offsets and leaves the group) and close pools, and the process exits 0. The order matters: readiness down, drain HTTP, then drain everything else. Pair this with the preStop hook and the termination grace period in the pod spec.

ops.find: The dirty set is the key idea — it tells the flusher what to drain. Failed batches go back on the set for retry.

ops._why: examples/25: /write-back/metrics/{id} answers 202; upsert; bounded retry (metric:attempts, metric:failed, backoff)

ops.text: Write-back has more moving parts than the other patterns; the slide shows the shape of Example 25. (1) PUT /write-back/metrics/{mid} writes the metric to a Redis hash, adds the id to a 'dirty set', which tells the flusher which ids still have to reach the database, and answers 202 Accepted: the value is queued, not yet durable. (2) The flusher runs as a background asyncio task: it SPOPs up to FLUSH_BATCH dirty ids and writes them in one executemany upsert (ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE), so an id flushed twice stays one row. SPOP is atomic, so two flusher instances each get a distinct subset of ids and the flusher scales out. (3) When the flush fails, each id's count in the metric:attempts hash goes up and the id goes back on the dirty set; after five attempts it moves to metric:failed with its value still in the cache and the failure in the log, so an outage never loses a write without a trace. The sleep between cycles doubles after each failed flush, from one second to at most eight. Caveats: this is only safe with Redis persistence (AOF, appendonly yes); without it a Redis crash loses unflushed writes. For data that must not be lost, use write-through. For high-throughput telemetry where losing the last second is acceptable, write-back is what lets the service scale.

ops.text: The shutdown sequence that prevents dropped requests during a rolling deploy, from Example 21. One SIGTERM starts it: (1) the handler flips a flag so /readyz returns 503 and Kubernetes stops sending new traffic, while /healthz stays 200; (2) the service keeps serving for DRAIN_DELAY_SECONDS so the load balancer's removal propagates; (3) the handler then hands over to uvicorn, which stops accepting and finishes in-flight requests within --timeout-graceful-shutdown; (4) the lifespan exit closes the pools and the process exits 0. The ordering matters: stop taking new work before draining existing work. This is the application half; Appendix H covers the Kubernetes half (preStop hook, terminationGracePeriodSeconds). Together they give zero-downtime rollouts.
